title: When Can I Drive After a Tummy Tuck or Mommy Makeover?
meta_description: Driving: often 1 to 2 weeks after a tummy tuck (Salemy, ASPS website), 2 to 3 weeks after a mommy makeover (The Aesthetic Society). Who drives the kids?
excerpt: A tummy tuck alone and a mommy makeover have different driving dates, and they get mixed up online. Here are the sourced figures side by side, five checks to pass before you drive, and how to plan who drives the kids until you can.
quick_answer:
When can I drive after a tummy tuck or mommy makeover?

You can often drive 1 to 2 weeks after a tummy tuck alone, according to Shahram Salemy, MD, on the ASPS website. After a mommy makeover, The Aesthetic Society says you may be comfortable driving in 2 to 3 weeks, or once all your sutures and drains are out and you no longer take pain medication. Your surgeon clears you.

sources.title: Mommy makeover aftercare and recovery
quotes: You may be comfortable enough to drive a car in two or three weeks or when all of your sutures and drains are removed, and you are no longer taking pain medication.
By the end of the first week, you should be walking around the house frequently, but you will still be unable to drive.
The first week will be the worst, and you may still feel like you are recovering for two to three weeks.
If you have small children, you must put someone else totally in charge of their care for at least two weeks.
You won't feel like yourself for at least seven to ten days, and you still shouldn't do any heavy lifting (such as picking up your children or baskets of laundry) for four to six weeks.
Arrange for someone to help you get around the house and help with your medication for at least the first 24 hours after surgery.
You will likely go for a follow-up evaluation with your surgeon within five days.
If you have traditional sutures, you will typically have these removed within the first week or two (absorbable sutures will not have to be removed).
Plan to take about two weeks off from work, depending on the physical demands of your job.
You will need to wear an abdominal binder after a tummy tuck.

notes: Full rewrite for the deciding reader, on the 3 Nov plan. Fixes the live '1-2 weeks' for a mommy makeover: The Aesthetic Society says two or three weeks; 1 to 2 weeks is Salemy's tummy tuck figure. All live claims without a source are gone (4-7 days, 10 days, 7-14 days, 7-10 days for short drives, 3-4 weeks for long trips, board-certified surgeons, phone, #contactus). Beyond the mommy makeover and tummy tuck facts files, each read tonight with its quote above: The Aesthetic Society on driving 10 to 14 days after a BBL (matches bbl.facts.ts work-10-14-days; the one line consistency.py flags) and Cleveland Clinic on a panniculectomy. Also new and read tonight: Florida Statutes 316.193, 316.614 and 893.03, and MedlinePlus on oxycodone. The Mittal abstract was read through NCBI E-utilities (efetch PMID 31858207), because PubMed's page blocks automated reads. Deviations: the plan's '1-3 week timing card' states the three sourced figures and never '1 to 3 weeks': no source gives that range, and it would blur the difference this rewrite exists to fix, so the 5 Oct meta description and excerpt were not used. The hero has no person: the blog template prints no 'Model shown. Not a patient.' label on heroes (images.md says it does; grep finds none in components/blog), so a model there would break the brief. The passenger photo is the one AI person, placed with Figure so it carries that caption. The first check says 'pain medication', The Aesthetic Society's words, not the 5 Oct 'prescription pain medicine'. build_sql.py only adds categories, so the live 'Breast Augmentation' and 'Liposuction' categories stay unless removed separately. Open: whether Alluring uses drains, its follow-up schedule and nights in Miami are owner questions, written around. Not yet in BLOG_V2_SLUGS. Fact check 2026-11-03: meta now attributes each figure to its own source (The Aesthetic Society's tummy tuck page gives no driving date); dropped the engine-off full wheel turn, which has no source and strains the arms and abdomen; padding now says ask first; 'free' dropped from the new consultation link (canon).
